description: Team from Türkiye working on the Martian Map challenge: a safety-first walking route planner for astronauts on Mars, built on NASA data. Team is complete.
summary: Marswalk Map is a web globe and route planner for landing and moving safely on Mars. The user picks a crewed or a robotic mission. The globe first screens the whole planet with NASA elevation, thermal inertia, albedo, radiation shielding and dust storm data, and shows why Jezero crater is a good, data-rich study site. Inside Jezero, the tool shows where the chosen lander can touch down, suggests the nearest suitable landing site for a clicked science target, and plans the fastest safe route for a suited astronaut, a crewed rover or a robotic rover. Every point of the route is checked against life support, walk-back, energy and distance limits, and the result is a clear GO / CAUTION / NO-GO decision. Every limit is traced to a NASA or mission source.
details:
The globe screens all of Mars with MOLA elevation, TES thermal inertia and albedo, radiation shielding and dust storm data. About 48% of the surface stays open for a crewed lander and 18% for a robotic lander. Jezero crater passes every test and has the richest terrain data, so it is our study area.

Inside Jezero we use two scales: an 86 x 107 km area at 20 m built from 64 USGS CTX terrain models for crewed missions, and the USGS 1 m HiRISE model of the delta sampled at 5 m for robotic missions. Landing maps mark each cell as landable, marginal or not landable from the steepest slope inside the lander's safe circle.

The user clicks a science target. The app suggests the nearest suitable landing site and A* finds the fastest route. At every point we check four things: the crew can still walk back if the vehicle fails (6.4 h of an 8 h suit), the battery brings the vehicle home with a 20% reserve, the base is no more than 10 km away, and the mission fits the suit time budget. The result is a clear GO / CAUTION / NO-GO decision, and a failing part of the route is marked with the reason.

Every limit is traced to a NASA or mission source, and each layer shows what it cannot see. We used only finished NASA and USGS products. The site runs fully in the browser with TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL, with routing in a Web Worker and no server. Data was prepared with GDAL, QGIS, Python and NASA Ames Stereo Pipeline.

Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/demirataalbuz-maker/martian-map
